en: The Compendium of the Four Aims, composed by the great poet Śrī Kṣemendra. First Chapter.
May this trunk of truth, sprinkled with the nectar purified by fresh compassion, possessing the shade of patience, adorned with the creeper of virtuous intelligence, rooted in ethical discipline,
and featuring sprouts shimmering with the growth of sentient beings, flourish for those who possess merit.
May Dharma, with its blossoming flowers of rising virtue and its fruit of glory, lead to auspiciousness.
For the instruction of disciples and for the satisfaction of the wise,
Kṣemendra composes this Compendium of Chapters using his own verses.
Dharma is the refuge for men both in this world and the next; Dharma is the sun in the darkness, capable of quelling all calamities; Dharma is the treasure-trove called "the well-disposed";
Dharma is the kinsman on the vast path where no kin exist; Dharma is the steadfast friend.
In the parched desert of the ocean of saṃsāra, there is no wish-fulfilling tree superior to Dharma.
In the ear, the discourse on Dharma; in the mouth, speech devoted to the delight of Dharma;
in the mind, the aspiration for Dharma; everywhere, the abiding in Dharma as one's companion;
and in the body, action consisting of Dharma—this is the equipment for the attainment of the auspicious.
Even at the time of the world's destruction, its shore-fruits remain untouched by even a fraction of calamity.

A birth devoid of human status is a contemptible birth for those whose delusion is fixed in the thickest darkness; a man lacking intelligence is destitute of auspicious fruits and his conduct is equal to that of beasts.
Intelligence, when bereft of true wisdom, wanders in the investigation of the reality of existence and non-existence.
Scholarship devoid of Dharma is merely fruitless exertion for those whose speech resembles that of a parrot.
That "wisdom" which belongs to those blinded by pride and serves only to destroy the excellence of others is nothing but an elephant's bath in a flood of the dust of envy.
That wisdom which takes away stainless virtue—desire does not do that; that fortitude by which the senses attain the power of tranquility—desire does not do that;
that cleverness by which the world-conquering illusion (māyā) is deceived—desire does not do that.
That is true wisdom by which one attains peace and overcomes the cycle of existence.
He alone is blind who is devoid of sacred learning; he alone is a rogue who brings no benefit to those who seek his help;
he alone is dead who possesses no reputation; and he alone is pitiable whose mind is not fixed on righteousness.
No benefit was ever performed for another, no wealth was given, nor was truth spoken;
that time when one's life reaches fruitlessness is the time for lamentation.
There is no wealth equal to generosity; there is no vow equal to truthfulness. There is no auspiciousness equal to ethical discipline; there is no benefit equal to patience.
Truthfulness in speech, a nature consisting of clarity in vision that brings solace to all hearts,
the relinquishing of gifts in hand, the thought of ending the suffering of one's own birth in the mind,
compassion alone as the beloved deeply attached to the heart, and the exertion for the sake of others in the body.
He alone among men truly lives, while others wandering in existence are as if lifeless.
For those whose minds are resolved upon protecting the lives of others, compassion alone is the mother of Dharma; it is the nectar of life for all people in the world,
and is declared by the sages, who possess the eye of wisdom, to be an extraordinary merit.
Non-violence is the praiseworthy path to one's own city of welfare within this cycle of existence.
For the constant protection of living beings, all actions are undertaken; yet there is nothing in all the worlds dearer than the lives of those very beings.
The merit of one who possesses perfect compassion cannot be calculated.
The virtuous person who observes the vow of non-violence grants fearlessness to all living beings.
That very best of men is the source of the splendor of the ornaments of sentient beings, the supreme ornament of the earth and the atmosphere;
in whose lotus-face Sarasvatī, ever-truthful and free from error, dwells eternally as an ornament.

May that wealth which is clung to like a wet garment, which yields no fruit for the seeker, and which acts as a thorn to others— wealth that is merely a cause of affliction and is defiled— go to its own destruction by itself!
And may this body, which is devoid of compassion and service to others, and has become a mere burden to the earth, likewise perish!
May that which is attached to its own self-interest and serves as an abode for a multitude of misfortunes never belong to anyone.
He who is worthy of worship by men and honored by the gods through his acts of accumulating merit and compassion—
he whose body has service to others as its sole ornament attains the very essence of existence.

He was free from desire for the wealth of others, devoid of curiosity regarding the wives of others, affectionate toward the requests of others, and firm in his forbearance toward the insults of others;
he was skilled in praising others and abandoned by the slander of the virtues of others.
Through abundant merit, a person becomes intent on removing the suffering of others.
The virtue of the good is like that of lotuses, for it is worthy of being the refuge of Fortune; that Fortune shines through generosity like the form of a noble elephant in rut;
and that generosity is ever filled with honor, like the new moon.
He is like grass who, through familiarity, does not wither away as he gradually dries up.
Wealth has its fruit in giving; sacred learning has its fruit in tranquility; the hand has its fruit in the worship of the gods;
action has its fruit in dharma; life has its fruit in the play of removing the suffering of others;
speech has its fruit in truth; and the exaltation of power has its fruit in the flourishing of the world’s happiness.
The intellect of those capable of liberation, which has as its fruit the contemplation of the cessation of existence, indeed leads to prosperity.
For those who cultivate moral conduct, who cherish their lineage, who practice sincerity, who avoid deceit, who value virtue, who fix their intellect upon the Dharma,
who contemplate forbearance, who pacify darkness, and who listen to the hearing of reality—
In this cycle of existence, I see no merit for the virtuous equal to that of benefiting others.
Setting aside pilgrimages that involve the exhaustion of long journeys and great expense, and rituals that are mere displays of grandeur,
as well as austerities that wither the body— may your minds delight in the cessation of violence.
The king is the ornament of the earth— a disciplined, pure, and self-controlled sage, an ascetic, a counselor, and a scholar— who,
like a companion, waters the garden of Dharma when it is being drenched by the showers of the water of virtuous deeds.
This is the full sowing of the seed for the future tree of the Kṛta age.
Hypocrisy, observance of vows, desirelessness, detachment, Vedic learning, and gentleness—
these roots of the tree of the Kali age remain hidden and deeply concealed by crookedness.
Whatever gifts the virtuous proclaim, whatever austerities and sacred fords there may be—
all that merit shines forth together in one place, as does great worthiness and, in another, freedom from desire.

For the virtuous, lack of wretchedness is the beauty of the face; freedom from greed is the nobility of speech and the absence of begging; not being fit for service is the mark of a body worthy of being served by the good; and having palms that do not turn upward is the characteristic of the hand.
One who is honorable is superior to one merely of noble birth; one who possesses the arts is superior to one born of noble lineage; a scholar is superior to one who knows the arts;
one of good character is superior to a scholar; a wealthy man is superior to one of good character; and a donor is superior even to a wealthy man—thus is fame won by the one who does not beg.

If non-violence—which exudes compassion—blooms through intense vows and austerities, what need is there for distant, essential pilgrimage sites? If the mind is pure with tranquility and purified by truth, what use are other efforts? If the intellect extends itself to the service of others, what is the use of other meritorious acts of giving?
What is the use of the application of means for liberation, if devotion is said to exist in those whose minds are pure?
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Praise of Dharma. Chapter Two:
Homage be to that [Buddha], the treasure-trove of the primary abodes, who bestows wealth even upon the virtuous through his exertion.
With such an intention, they bring the virtues of kings who are devoid of merit to a state of exhaustion before [the assembly].
The practice of giving and other virtues is performed with wealth; through wealth, the fortunate obtain further wealth.
Without wealth, even talk of desire does not exist; wealth alone is the root of the three aims of life, and nothing else.
That which is prescribed as a fierce battle-game by eunuchs using fighting cocks; that which is long relished by fools as a pleasant pastime—the warbling of poets and parrots;
and that wherein the lowly and the exalted alike are driven like horses by their master.
That has acted with excessive pride toward wealth, which is but the abode of the dance of fleeting enjoyment.
Worship is achieved through wealth alone, not by noble lineage; fame is achieved through wealth alone, not by valor;
beauty is achieved through wealth alone, not by youth; and religious action is achieved through wealth alone, not by mere life.

The elderly, the renowned, the wise, the learned, the brave, those versed in the Vedas, the poets, and the noble-born—beholding the face of one who possesses wealth, they always say, "Victory! and "Long life!"
With eyes whose lashes were motionless and filled with anger, he was like a god rendered agitated by silence;
a low-born man, humble and bowing with palms joined, praised him while longing for wealth.
Therefore, one should strive for the acquisition of wealth not yet obtained, for the protection and regulation of what has been acquired,
for the constant increase of what is being protected, and for the distribution and expenditure of what has increased.
The Dharmādhāna [year], which possesses the moon’s purity and restraint, is for the attainment of beloved ones, friends, kinsmen, status, energy, prosperity, victory, life-force, knowledge, and arts;
it is praiseworthy at the time of bodily tranquility and in an undisputed partition.
When wealth is relinquished, the continuous binding of knots does not occur for the virtuous.
Socializing with parasites, wandering among troupes of bards, delighting in courtesans, smelling the scent of the virtuous,
competing with the well-dressed, and shame regarding one’s own livelihood— these are the primary causes of the destruction of wealth.
A wife devoid of virtue, a spendthrift, a circle of friends full of deceit, an insatiable teacher, relatives impoverished despite heaps of wealth and enjoyments,
a servant devoted to theft and violence, and a son who is wicked— these are the ones by whom one is cast down by the treacherous.
Thus, this destruction of the accumulated store attained through hundreds of afflictions is directly perceived.
Skill is the root of wealth; association with wise counsel is the watering of the garden of prosperity; boldness rains down jewels; self-restraint uproots the forest of calamities;
the guarding of secrets protects fortune; the concealment of counsel pacifies misfortune; and the avoidance of the wicked is essential.
Indolence is the unbearable frost that withers the lotus-forest of men's wealth.
Inability to endure cold, fear of the sun's heat, concern for reputation, waiting for travelers on the road,
shame, pride, being momentarily face-to-face with others, and preoccupation with astrology— these are the obstacles to wealth.
The wearing of finery, anxiety over various hardships, obstructing others, and the arrogance of self-indulgence—
these are the losses regarding wealth when there is delay in its acquisition, like fruits from rivers that flow swiftly away.
The wealth of the ignorant is consumed by teachers and astrologers; that of merchants, by those clever at embezzlement and thieves; and that of kings, by hosts of scribes and singers.
By poverty a family perishes; by pride, one's virtue; by hatred, the fruit of learning;
by association with the wicked, one's character; by immoral conduct, one's fame;
by laziness, wealth goes to ruin; and by fickleness, the height of honor.
And by the acceptance of the wretchedness of begging, the entire multitude of virtues of men is destroyed.
Even the joy of the Raghus met with calamity through childishness; Bāṇa through negligence; Bali through straightforwardness;
Nala through bad association; and the son of Yayāti through an inability to endure hardship.
Folly, negligence, lack of trust, bad company, and fear of hardship—
these five defects cause the contraction of prosperity, just as they do for a lotus pond.
The wealth obtained by men who hang between the pits of wicked kings flows away through the unguarded apertures called the sense-faculties, just as water leaks from jars that have holes.
Bees are imprisoned within the lotus heart for its delicious and fresh fragrance;
moths meet their destruction by constantly falling into the lamp out of a passion for its form;
deer fall by the very sound of song; and elephants are led to their end by the touch of a female elephant.
Therefore, it is attachment to the senses alone that suddenly acts as the messenger of calamity for men.

By those who have failed to acquire wealth and have instead squandered what they possessed, their family has been defiled by ignoble livelihoods, the multitude of their virtues has been reduced to the value of mere straw, and the axe has been laid at the very root of their honor.
Born into a noble family, he became humble before the lowly; through the insults of service, he fell into a state of misery.
By his betrayal of his own honor and reputation, the fire of a curse was kindled.
Because of that malady, he consumed the poison of begging placed into his own hand.
That wealth which was not protected by him has ended up gazing upon the face of an enemy.
A virtuous man runs to serve even a base person; therefore, that base person attains a value equal to a jewel through his virtues, yet no one accepts those virtues.
Begging is a great thunderbolt to one's honor; nothing at all is gained by it, for wealth is not produced thereby.
What indeed is not undertaken by one who regards wealth as wealth? Blessed is he who possesses it.
The study of sciences and arts, service to kings,
the arduous toil of wandering through paths across regions, islands, and mountains,
and even military expeditions on this earth— all these are undertaken out of greed for obtaining food.
"It is obtainable through wealth"—such is the common saying among those who possess riches.
As long as a person’s belly is not momentarily emaciated by hunger, there arises a desire for liberation through the delightful discourse on Dharma;
but when the time for thinking of food arrives, wealth becomes the cause [of thought] without any other motive.
In the Dharma, whose intellect remembers what? Who remembers whom? And by what is the ground of liberation perceived?
The hypocrite, skilled in harsh chatter, seeks to attract wealth; he knows no other way than the shameless recitation of false praises of his own virtues, for he cannot endure others' excellence.
A noble man would not act thus, owing to his family, discipline, and virtue; therefore, he remains mute when it comes to soliciting wealth.
Indeed, for one who possesses sharp arrows, there is the attainment of a hundred thousand [coins] in the presence of the king.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Praise of the Meaning.
The third chapter:
[He] whose tremulous eyes rise up at the playful movements of charming women—

May the dark form of the Flower-Arrowed One (Kāma) extend happiness to you— a form that seems as if anointed by the shimmering masses of bees with the luster of blue lotus forests, and which appears as if veiled by the wings of his fragrant friends, the bees.
With the luster of blossoming *ketakī* flowers and wandering bees,
like necklaces of pearls released from their blue sapphire central gems,
her eyes are marked by thick lashes like the crescent of the moon.
Victorious are the splashes of nectar-and-poison from the eyes of those with gazelle-like eyes.
They say that the foremost fruit of wealth is sacrifice, and the fruit of sacrifices is merit free from dispute.
The full fruit of merit is the world of Indra; and for women, the heavenly vault itself consists of sixteen-year-old maidens.
These are the rows of bow-like eyebrows, curved with the playful gestures of young women, and these are the arrows of the third parts of their eyes, reaching as far as the ears;
they have been burnt by the enemy of Andhaka (Śiva) due to the onset of fresh agitation in his mind.
Out of impetuosity, without any reflection, this wretched Cupid acts solely through falsehood.
The bow of the Mind-born [Cupid], bent with shame, surpasses them by the play of her eyebrows; the moon reaches a state of thinness through the luster of her face, which is pale with anxiety;
and the lotus-stalk sinks low before the two creepers of her arms, radiant with laughter.
With her sidelong glances, she renders the cluster of blue water-lilies pale and lusterless.
There must surely be some instruction from the thunderbolt within the hearts of those made of iron,
by which they have endured the glances of bold women cast as far as their ears.
Her tremulous side-glances consist of blue lotuses; her eyebrows are composed of waves; her face consists of a hundred moons; her limbs are made of lotus stalks;
her touch is made of sandalwood; and her smile consists of frost.
Does she, as if composed of fire, cause distress through her memory?

Whose minds are not shaken by the side-long glances of her whose eyes are sharp as the arrows of Love— glances that possess mature shafts and which serve to instill the zeal for the desire to conquer the people of the three worlds?
The friendship of the ears remains steadfast even among those who are most fickle.
Upon the breast-regions of beautiful women, which captivate the heart, and upon their hips adorned with girdles,
there appears a manifold array of lines depicting the ever-fresh play of pride in their special ornaments.
The breasts of his beloved, marked with sandalwood paste and possessing the pure luster of fly-whisks in the form of her shimmering, playful smiles; and her beautiful hips, radiant as gold,
which serve as the throne for kings.
This empire consists of victory and defeat, but the remainder is composed of anxiety.
By the deer, firm in their vow of forest-dwelling, the various glances and movements of the eyes of that fawn-eyed woman were observed;
oh, how her radiance [now shines] due to her addiction to the brilliance of the sun!
Not even by casting oneself into fire was it ever obtained through gold.

The line of hair on her body, marked by three curves, shines like a strand of *śaivala* moss fallen upon the beaks of swans from a necklace resting unevenly due to the rise of her newly developed breasts.
This is not the triple fold of the young woman clinging to the waves; it is the line of hair that shines forth.
Having bathed in this pool of amorous play, the moon has departed, leaving behind its streak of dark spots.

To a slender-limbed woman in separation, the time of the onset of winter is a swarm of scorching needles in her ears—the sweet warbling of female cuckoos; it is a fierce forest fire in the blossoming groves of *aśoka*, *palāśa*, and *campaka* trees; what else could it be to men?
Love itself is the guest who inhales the fragrance of the swarm of bees that is the eradication of the body.
In the moon-like face of the long-eyed Hariṇī during separation, paleness— the companion of the fame of Love— attains full maturity;
it is intensified by the corners of her eyes, reddened by the flow of incessant tears.
Of her who bore Love as if his majesty were eclipsed.
In separation from the slender-limbed one— the subduer of the heart, the abode of wretchedness,
the dense cloud, the fire of passion fueled by love for her husband, the mountain of pride, the extinguisher of the distress of anxiety, and the very departure of life— [the moon rises].
Her body, withered by the heat, turns toward her bed of lotus leaves.
When my beloved fell at my feet out of courtesy and affection, yet was not looked upon by me,
you saw the blazing fire of a curse, a harbinger of his exile, consuming his life-breaths.
Now that he is thus distressed with agitation, what is the use of these false consolations?
O friend, surely it was you yourself who gave me this counsel that leads only to my torment.
When her husband has arrived— having traversed the long journey that usually takes many days— the beautiful-eyed woman, free from obstacles on his way,
herself joyfully sheds tears and, full of respect, takes hold of the horse.
The dust clinging to his shoulders was shaken off by the flapping of the corners of his own garment.
The garment has become loose from trembling, the forehead is devoid of its tilaka mark, the face is covered with perspiration,
and the sprout-like lower lip, bitten by him, withers under the heat of his sighs;
O messenger, when your words reach the presence of that deceitful and hard-hearted man, they meet with frustration.
Out of affection for me, how much distress have you, provoked by anger, allowed to enter?
When the quarters were pervaded by the flame of the *aśoka* tree,
with arrows falling incessantly and the forest thickets blocked by nets of blossoms, the way of the traveler-deer was lost.
The *sahakāra* tree blossoms, the *karṇikāra* is difficult to endure, the bees have abandoned the *sindhuvāra*, and it smiles;
alas! out of fear of separation, [the bee] clings to the neck of the beloved woman.
Alas, what Kāpālika abandons at the onset of autumn?
When her beloved resolved to forcibly loosen the girdle during their first union,
the slender-limbed woman’s nectar-like tears rolled upon her neck; agitated by the trembling of her expanding breaths,
they resembled the humming of bees pressed against closing lotuses— tears that were yet powerless to resist.
The fortunate ones scatter their words, "Nana-nē," for a moment, filled with the sound of "huṃ" due to their inability to speak further.
Her creeper-like limbs rendered motionless by a firm embrace, the young woman— her sprout-like curls held back by her lover as he forcibly pressed his lips to her lotus-face—
closed her eyes, while her trembling, quivering, and reddened petal-like lower lip quivered.
I think he is practicing the recitation of that mantra which gives birth to the life of him who was born from Mānasa.

By whom alone are these arrows of the Beloved of Rati— arrows whose quills are like the flickering crests of peacocks, whose great renown lies in shattering the silence of proud women, whose feathers are the sighs of separated wives, and whose tips are as sharp as the sidelong glances from the eyes of beautiful women— not endured?
They produce hissing sounds and the whistling of sighs from young women whose sprout-like lower lips are bitten.
May the pair of eyes of the deer-eyed women extend their lives further;

may the continuity of your smile [extend] their fame; and may the slopes of their breasts and hips [extend] the splendor of their broad hips—since the two mountains, the deer-eyed women, have offered these as drums for the Lord’s conquest of the three worlds.
Thus, I know that my mother’s blessings were bestowed for the sake of enduring effort and for my welfare.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Praise of Desire.
The fourth chapter:
[The world] is agitated by no small amount of sorrow due to the loss of enjoyments, their non-enjoyment, and through anger and strife.
We praise discernment (*viveka*), which— though it may at will follow the path of desire, which is contrary to the abode of desire,

and though it follows disjunction, being as uneven as the ripening of the transformations of disease and vomiting— is the sole irrigation for the tree of doubt regarding the fruit of liberation, once the pains of the eyes have been uprooted.

In a garden, the moonlight, the song of a moon-faced woman, and the excellent conversation of friends— who would not find these to be a source of exceeding happiness, raining down supreme joy that is the companion of bliss?
Yet, this [joy] is [threatened] by the tongues of serpents that are the company of the wicked, and by the flapping of the ears of elephants that are [the influence of] the base.
It is like the net of Indra, resembling a flock of birds with wings flapping at the corners of her mature eyes.
Childhood is struck down by a mass of unbearable delusion; youth is overflowing with passion;
and old age is agitated by the thorn of the failure of all sensory enjoyments—always sorrowful and devoid of pure light without renunciation.
Alas, for those wandering again and again in saṃsāra, their lives have passed away in vain.
Childhood behavior was seen, then the pride of youth, and then the renunciation of old age; that too has passed, that too has passed, and even this has passed—it is all like a dream or an illusion.
There is no other thing as defiled as affection, which is the cause of thousands of repeated births;
it causes both man and the lamp to remain intent on service and devoted to the distribution of household goods.
The royal palace is overrun by sycophants; the house of learning by the envious; wealth by anxieties; the family by wicked sons through various afflictions;
happiness by the insults of deceiving rogues; and the mind by thousands of cares, which destroy its goodness.
Therefore, there is nothing at all that is not turbid with anger, except for the one faultless tranquility.
In wealth there is the fear of disease; in pleasure, the fear of its decay; in riches, the fear of fire and the sovereign;
in servitude, the fear of the master; in virtue, the fear of the wicked; in one's lineage, the fear of a bad wife;
in honor, the fear of humiliation; in victory, the fear of enemies; and in the body, the fear of Death.
Everything in existence is indeed fear; alas, only dispassion is freedom from fear.
Those who have quenched their minds— whose intense thirst has ceased— with the water of peace,
and who are the steadfast leaders capable of rescuing others from the defeat of cyclic existence, do not partake of the thick streams of milk flowing from the breasts of their mothers.
Furthermore, men [perceive] that mouth which was once fond of the breast as now devoid of teeth.
Alas, having cast aside the nectar-like bliss of contentment— the very means for pleasing others—
how strange it is that men instead cherish honors and riches as the primary means for the pleasure of deep sleep!
When solitude is within one's own power, when traveling to secluded places leads to the pacification of rebirth,
and when the transformation of worldly existence makes even the avoidance of calamities easy—
then shame stands before the virtuous man at the very moment of birth, as if it were blood.
If he again places his hand upon his head, thinking "it is my nurse," he falls.

Those blinded by passion do not desist from this evil path called the enjoyment of women— a source of exhaustion, bitter in its consequences, and a ground for shame and loathing— having fallen into it;
yet, if they possessed even a moment of discernment regarding their own mind, they would reflect upon its power to draw them back.
This person never turns his face away from those other than Rati.

In the cremation ground that is the body— thick with hair, possessing skulls as mounds of red dye-mud, and displaying prominent bones for teeth— the world of lustful men, agitated by desire, takes its pleasure among women.
Oh, how the courtesan of craving, who deludes all people, is both clever and yet deceiving; she robs the helpless and innocent of their wealth of tranquility!
She is skilled at initiating one into calamity with her tremulous pupils that cannot endure being gazed upon—she who is the beloved of misfortune.
With sidelong glances that are like deceptive dice, these rogues of passion are crooked with guile.
Childhood is a state of delusion caused by one's mother and father; youth is the pursuit of pleasure with unchaste and beautiful women;
and even old age is filled with wicked wives and sons.
Truly, there is nothing here but this wondrous friend.
To whom do they not offer instruction on tranquility? For unions with loved ones are like dreams;
youth is swallowed up by old age, and lives are bitten by Death.
If one were to reflect upon the royal sages such as Rāma, Nahuṣa, and Śveta, what would be gained by them, whose stories have faded through the vast calculations of time?
Let those of immense power who were seen with our own eyes and yet have perished be counted instead.
Therefore, knowing that everything is swallowed up by impermanence, let tranquility be remembered.
When Fortune is fickle, when the king is like a forest deer in a hunting ground, when she is but a dream, as fleeting as the flash of lightning from a dense cloud in youth,
and when Time is indeed a bee for the honey of the filaments of the lotus-like people; [then one should seek refuge in the Lord].
Then, in this saṃsāra, the mind of the unawakened does not find rest.
The peahen of desire drinks the still and clear water of contentment;
the deer of the inner mind, having wandered within, finds rest inside;
and this [mind], dissolved in the cool water of the tree of tranquility, [overcomes] the exhaustion of its feverish heat.
The lordly elephant of the intoxicated mind, its passion closing, inevitably abandons [its objects].
When enjoyments have passed into the path of memory and one is attached to various separations,

grief touches the mind only slightly— not at all— in those who are entirely free from distress; for indeed, to those who perceive everything within as finite, everything within becomes truly finite in due course.
For the most part, our certainty regarding the thorough understanding of the exhaustion of the body is profound.
Let the season of flowers manifest its abundance of fragrances;
let the breezes dwelling on the Malaya mountains blow constantly, sporting in the sky;
and let Love exhaust my fortitude at will with the side-glances of the long-lashed-eyed woman.
May peace, the companion of unwavering bliss within the unchanging mind, be mine.
When the conceit of being fortunate has been swallowed by old age, when the spreading creeper of prosperity has withered away,
when pride has slackened in the acquisition of wealth, and when steadfastness is established in that which is called tranquility;
When youth has passed away along with passion, when enjoyments have gone together with desires,
and when the body has dissolved along with delusion— then this path to liberation becomes unobstructed.
The mind is like dust scattered by the wind; physical form is like the heat of the sun at day’s end;
enjoyment is as fleeting as the shackles of a house in a miserable state; youth is but the smile of a flower;
the meeting with kinsmen is a dream; and even this body is a mere well of merit for the journey ahead.
For the virtuous who constantly contemplate this, the fetters of existence no longer arise.
He for whom gain and loss are indistinguishable, who is devoid of distinguishing between friend and foe, who regards honor and contempt as equal, and for whom pleasure and pain are identical;
he is neither a silent sage nor a non-silent sage, his mind resting equally upon the forest and water.
One who is free from both virtue and vice is touched neither by wretchedness nor by its absence.
That [beauty] is far from yellow sandalwood; has it not been lost by the necklace?

Is it not easily found upon the orb of a beloved’s breast? Where could it be when the moon is impoverished? There is no meeting with song at all, nor is there any equality with it in the case of the Siddhamadhura [bee].
The joy that suddenly unfolds in the mind when despair has been brought about;
Having attained the limit of the nectar of true happiness, my desires fulfilled by the wonder of fresh joy,
I am as if relieved of a burden through the renunciation of all grasping and accumulation.
The constant preoccupation with acquiring wealth, a forest of desires planted within the heart, the futile wearing down of the feet, the service of the wicked and the miserly,
perpetual lamentation over calamities, and a face dejected by separation from loved ones— [all these are the fruits of worldly life].
Leaving behind his home and bathing, the meritorious man goes to a secluded place.

There is no other bringer of well-being than the Dharma for living beings whose souls are devoted to it; there is no other way of life equal to wealth that is capable of pacifying the suffering of misfortune.
In this cycle of existence, nothing else is so supremely blissful or beautiful as the face of a woman.
What indeed is superior to liberation, which is the flavor of the cessation resulting from the destruction of all afflictions?
By whatever merit has been acquired by Kṣemendra through his instruction on the four aims of life, may this world become a vessel for those four aims.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Praise of Liberation.
This *Caturvargasamgraha* is now complete.
